title: I accidentally built a motion-analysis tool because animating my point-and-click protagonist was driving me insane
author: milox88
selftext:
I'm working on a 2D point-and-click adventure heavily inspired by 90s games, especially Broken Sword.

I hit what was becoming the biggest production bottleneck: character animation. I wanted that very specific hand-drawn/raster 90s adventure-game feel, but getting consistent poses and walk cycles from AI-generated frames was... not going well.
Then I had an idea.

I own the original Broken Sword on Steam. Instead of trying to eyeball its animation, I started reverse-engineering my local game resources for study/reference purposes.

..and that rabbit hole escalated quickly.

I ended up extracting 19,363 character frames from 687 character resources, with 19,363/19,363 frames successfully decoded, then catalogued them into animation sequences. George alone turned out to contain a pretty elaborate animation system: 8-direction walking, standing, turning walks, slow-in/slow-out transitions, turns, interactions, etc.


So I built (well..i argued for a whole afternoon with Chatgpt, asking to build python scripta) a Motion Atlas, a local tool that turns all of this into a searchable motion-reference library.

I can browse animations frame-by-frame, play them at their original-ish timing, inspect silhouettes and N→N+1 transitions, assign a reference animation to one of my own characters, and then put the original reference frame and my character's PNG side by side for validation.

The idea isn't to copy Broken Sword's characters or ship any of its assets. None of this material goes into the game. I'm using it as a private animation/motion reference — basically a very elaborate digital animation bible.


My pipeline is becoming:
motion reference → my character → produce frames → compare in Atlas → approve/reject → iterate

And, weirdly, this might have solved one of the biggest problems in the whole project.
The funniest part is that I'm not really a programmer or an animator. This entire tool exists because at some point I thought: “Wait... the finished animation data I want to study is literally sitting inside the game files.”


Next step is to let Codex handle the tedious animation process. I will give it a couple of .PNG files as reference for my character and let it produce the animation making a raster via Krita/Opentoonz.

..well, i hope that.
